summary: This unit teaches you to room a guest from the front desk to the room: prepare for arrivals, greet the guest, handle the luggage safely, lead the way, show and explain the room, deal with problems such as a room that is not ready, and record what you did. You will also learn how rooming differs for groups, VIPs, guests with special needs and guests at a private villa.

blocks.p: **Rooming** means taking a guest from the front desk to their room, showing them the room and its features, and leaving them comfortable and safe. It is the guest's first long contact with the property after check-in, and it often decides whether they feel welcome.

This unit is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees who work as bell attendants, front desk agents, villa hosts or guest service staff. At a large hotel a bell attendant usually rooms the guest. At a small guest house or private villa, the same person may check the guest in, carry the bags and explain the house.

What this means in practice
rows: Prepare for arrivals
Read the arrivals list for names, times and special requests
Check that the room is clean, inspected and ready
Make sure cots, amenities and other requests are in place
Greet and start the rooming
Greet the guest by name and give your own name
Receive the key folder without saying the room number aloud
Check the luggage with the guest
Handle luggage safely
Lift, load and carry bags without hurting yourself or the guest's belongings
Tag and count every piece
Lead the guest to the room
Walk slightly ahead and to one side
Point out facilities and manage the lift
Adapt to a tired or hurried guest
Show and explain the room
Knock, enter, place the bags, and explain the main features
Explain safety features, the safe and the fire plan
Solve problems
Room not ready, wrong beds, a fault or an unhappy guest
Apologise and call the desk
Close the rooming and record it
Ask if the guest needs anything else and leave quietly
Record the rooming and report faults and special occasions
Adapt to different guests and places
Groups, VIPs, families, guests with special needs, private villas

flow: Prepare before arrival
Greet and take the key folder
Check and load the luggage
Lead the guest to the room
Open the room and place the bags
Explain the room
Ask, leave and record

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and practical tasks: a role play rooming a guest in the Centre's mock room, and planning and carrying out a family's arrival at a villa. The assessor watches your greeting, safe lifting, the way you lead, what you explain, how you solve a problem, and the records you keep.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: Rooming is done with real people, so be polite and calm, and never say the guest's room number aloud where others can hear it.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Good rooming starts before the guest walks in. A guest taken to a room that is not ready, or whose request was forgotten, remembers that more than anything else about the stay.
The **arrivals list** shows who is arriving today. Read it at the start of your shift.

head: It shows
What you do with it
rows: Guest names and number of guests
Learn the names, so that you can greet each guest correctly.
**ETA** (estimated time of arrival)
Plan your time and make sure staff and the room are ready by then.
Room type and number
Check that it is the right type (for example a king bed or two single beds).
Special requests (cot, quiet room, ground floor, allergies, anniversary)
Pass them to housekeeping and the kitchen in time, and make sure the request is done before the guest arrives.
VIP or repeat guest marks
Prepare any extra attention the property's standard requires.

ul: A **VIP** (very important person) may get a welcome amenity such as fruit and a card, as the property's standard says. Do not add anything the property does not allow.
A **walk-in** is a guest who arrives without a booking. The front desk decides which room to give.
A **tour group** has a **rooming list**: a list of which room each member will have.

blocks.p: The front desk and housekeeping use short codes to show the state of each room. Codes differ between properties. These are common.

head: Code
Meaning
Can you room a guest in it?
rows: VC
Vacant and clean: the room is empty and cleaned, ready to be inspected or sold.
Only when it is also inspected and ready, as the property says.
VD
Vacant and dirty: the room is empty but still needs cleaning.
No.
OC
Occupied and clean.
No: a guest is in it.
OD
Occupied and dirty.
No.
OOO (out of order)
The room cannot be sold because it needs repair.
No.
Inspected / ready
A supervisor or housekeeper has checked the room.
Yes.

ul: Check on the system or with the desk that the room is shown as **clean and inspected** before you take a guest to it. This stops guests being taken to a room that is not ready.
If the room is not ready, tell the desk **before** you set out. The desk will offer another room, or invite the guest to wait.

head: Request
Set-up before arrival
rows: Baby cot
Placed in the room when it is prepared, before the guest arrives; check the cot is clean, safe and has a clean mattress.
Extra bed (**rollaway**)
A folding bed on wheels, made up with clean linen and placed where it will not block the door.
Connecting rooms
Two rooms side by side with a door between them: check that both rooms are ready and the door unlocks properly.
Allergy, diet or special need
Pass it to housekeeping and the kitchen; note it on the arrivals list.
Honeymoon or anniversary
An amenity or card if the property allows, and tell the desk and housekeeping.
Ground floor or quiet room
Check availability early, so the guest does not have to move later.

ul: Be neat: clean uniform, name badge, clean shoes, tidy hair, short clean nails.
Have a luggage trolley ready, with straps if the property uses them, and luggage tags.
Know the property: where the restaurant, pool, gym, spa, lifts, ice machines, stairs and fire exits are, and the opening times and services.
Know the day's events: weather, any maintenance, the restaurant's special, and the name of the duty manager.

sections.title: Greeting the guest and handling luggage

ul: Come forward, **smile**, and greet the guest. Use the guest's name from the arrivals list or the folder.
Give your **own name**, so the guest knows who is helping them: 'Good afternoon, Mr Brown. Welcome to the villa. I am Nadine and I will take you to your room.'
Use **title and surname** (Mr Brown, Mrs Campbell, Dr Reid) unless the guest asks you to use a first name.
Use a warm, clear voice and look at the guest. Offer to take the luggage.
A guest who looks tired after a long flight needs a short, simple rooming. Offer to explain more later.

blocks.h: The key folder and the room number

blocks.p: The desk agent gives you a **key card folder** (or key) for the guest. The room number is **written on the folder** and shown quietly to the guest. **Never say the room number aloud**: someone nearby could hear it and know exactly which room to go to, which is a risk for the guest.
At a hotel with bell staff, the **bell attendant** takes the luggage on a trolley. At a small guest house or villa, you may carry the bags yourself or the guest may do so.

flow: Ask the guest which pieces are theirs and count them
Look at each piece with the guest and note any damage
Attach a luggage tag to each bag, with the guest's name and room
Load the trolley safely
Ask the guest to check that every piece is there, before you leave the lobby

head: Check
Why
rows: Number of pieces, counted with the guest
So that nothing is lost and you can prove how many you took.
Damage already on a bag, pointed out with the guest
If a bag arrives damaged later, there is a record that you noted what was there.
Fragile or valuable items
Handle with extra care; the guest may prefer to carry them.
Tags with name and room
So that bags go to the right room if they travel by another route.

ul: **Heavy cases at the bottom, fragile and light ones on top.** Keep the stack steady so it does not tip.
Do not overload: if the trolley is hard to push or the pile is above your eyes, make two trips.
Balance the load and keep it close to the front of the trolley, with the handle clear.
If a guest wants to carry a handbag, laptop bag, medicine or valuables, **respect her wish** and carry the other bags.

flow: Check the weight: if it is too heavy, ask for help or use a trolley
Stand close, feet apart, one foot slightly ahead
Bend your **knees**, keep your **back straight**
Hold the load **close** to your body
Lift smoothly with your legs, without twisting
Put it down the same way

blocks.note: Bad lifting causes back injuries that can end your career. Never bend from the waist with straight legs, never twist while holding a load, and never carry more than you can see over.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Wear flat, closed, non-slip shoes.
Check the floor in front of you for wet patches, steps and cables.
Push a trolley rather than pull it. Go slowly round corners, and watch for children and guests.

sections.title: Leading the guest to the room

ul: Walk **slightly ahead and to one side**, so that you can lead and still talk to the guest. Look back now and then. Keep to the guest's pace.
Keep to the sides of corridors, and keep luggage trolleys away from guests who are walking.
Be friendly but brief. Match your talk to the guest: some like to chat, others are tired and quiet. Never ask personal questions.
**Point out facilities on the way**: the restaurant, bar, pool, gym, spa, business centre, shop, the lifts and the way to the beach, with opening times if you know them.

head: Situation
What you do
rows: The guest asks a question you cannot answer
Say you will find out and let them know soon, then do so. Never guess.
The guest is very tired
Keep it short, offer to explain more later, and leave them to rest.
The guest is in a hurry
Show only the essentials: safe, air conditioning, phone, fire plan. Offer the rest later.
The guest wants to chat
Be friendly, but do not delay other work.
A guest asks for a recommendation (restaurant, tour)
Give one or two suggestions that the property offers or approves.

ul: Hold the door and let the guest **enter first**. Then enter with the trolley. In most lifts, stand near the controls.

If the lift is small and the guest has a lot of luggage, send the **bags in another lift** (or the **service lift**, used by staff and for luggage, not by guests) and meet the guest at the room. If you do this, be sure the bags are tagged, and that the guest knows where they will be.
Keep your trolley from blocking the doors. Let guests with wheelchairs, prams or walking aids use the lift first.
On the way, if the lift stops or alarm sounds, stay calm and use the emergency button or phone.
Offer to help guests on stairs, and watch for wet surfaces on walkways outside, which can be slippery after rain or near the pool.
At a villa or cottage, walkways and steps may be outside and dark: carry a torch after dark and offer your arm when needed.

sections.title: In the room: opening it and explaining it

flow: Stop outside the door and **knock**, announcing 'Front desk' or 'Bell service' if the property says
Wait a moment, knock again, and then open the door with the key
Open the door fully and turn on the lights
**Step aside** and let the guest enter first
Place the luggage on the **luggage rack**, not on the bed
Put the key card in the slot if the room needs it for power

blocks.p: You knock even though the room should be empty, because it may have been let in error and be in use. Opening a door on a guest who is dressing is embarrassing and can lead to a complaint.

blocks.h: Check the room as you enter

ul: Is it clean, tidy and cool? Are the bed, towels and bathroom as they should be?
Do the lights, television, air conditioning, taps and toilet work?
Is anything broken, missing or left by a previous guest?
Is the room the type that was booked (the right beds)?
Is the requested cot, extra bed or amenity in place?

head: Feature
What you show
Why it matters
rows: Key card slot
Put the key card in the slot to switch on the power. Taking it out turns it off.
The guest cannot use lights or air conditioning without it, and may think there is a fault.
Air conditioning
The controls, and how to change the temperature or fan speed.
It is the first thing most guests want to adjust, and a wrong setting causes complaints.
Lights and switches
The main switches, bedside lamps and any master switch.
So the guest is not left in the dark.
Telephone
How to call the front desk, room service and an outside line, from the phone card.
The guest can ask for help or in an emergency.
In-room safe
How to set a private code: show the steps and look away. Do not watch the guest's code.
The guest keeps valuables safe and trusts you.
Fire escape plan
The plan inside the door shows the route out from that room. Point out the nearest exit.
In a fire the guest must know how to leave.
Door locks, chain and peephole
How to lock and chain the door; the **peephole** (the small lens in the door) to see who is outside.
The guest feels safe and does not open to strangers.
Balcony or patio door
How to lock it.
Keeps the room and the guest's things secure.
Minibar
Where the price list is and that items taken are charged.
Avoids a surprise on the bill.
Wi-Fi
The network name and the **password**.
Most guests want the internet at once.
Do Not Disturb sign
It asks staff not to knock or enter for now; how to hang it.
Gives the guest privacy and uninterrupted rest.
Guest directory
The folder or booklet with services, phone numbers and menus.
Guests can find out for themselves.
Television and remote
How to switch on, change channels, and any info channel.
A simple help that is often asked.
Bathroom
Hot and cold taps, shower control, hairdryer and towels.
Guests may not know how the shower works.
Wake-up call
How to book one with the desk, and the check-out time.
Stops guests missing flights and tours.

blocks.note: Jamaica's power is mostly 110 V at 50 Hz, with flat two-pin sockets (as in North America). Guests from Europe and some other countries may need a plug adapter, and some equipment is made for 220 V. If a guest asks, say what the room offers and refer them to the desk. Never advise on equipment you are unsure about.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.h: Explain what the guest needs, not everything

ul: Do not give a long speech. A short, calm explanation of the features above takes three or four minutes.
Ask 'Is there anything I can show you again?' and let the guest ask questions.
Tell the guest how to reach the desk, and what hours services such as room service and the restaurant run.
Show the room's safety features: the fire plan, the locks and the safe.

flow: Ask 'Is there anything else I can do for you?'
Wish the guest an enjoyable stay
If the guest offers a tip, thank them and follow the property's tipping policy
Leave and close the door gently and quietly behind you
Record the rooming

blocks.p: Even with careful preparation, things go wrong. The guest watches how you react. Stay calm, **apologise**, and act at once, because a problem fixed quickly and politely is often remembered as good service.

head: Problem
What you do
rows: The room has not been cleaned, or is not what was booked
Apologise, step out with the guest and call the desk
Take the guest back to the lobby or a comfortable place to wait, or to the new room the desk offers
Do not ask the guest to wait in a dirty room
The guest booked a king bed and the room has two single beds
Apologise, and call the desk to arrange the right room
Never say it is the guest's mistake
Something is broken (a leaking tap, air conditioning, television)
Tell the guest that it will be reported, and then report it to the desk or maintenance
If it cannot be fixed quickly, ask the desk to offer another room
The guest dislikes the view or the position of the room
Call the front desk to see what is available
Do not promise a change yourself
A guest asks something you do not know
Say you will find out and let them know soon; then do so
A guest is rude or upset
Stay polite and calm; do not argue
Listen, apologise for the problem, and tell your supervisor
You find a guest's property left in the room
Do not touch it; report it to the desk
Record it in the log

ul: You do not have to be able to fix every problem, but you do have to **report it** and follow it up.
If the room needs to be changed, the desk gives the guest a new key. Never give a room to a guest yourself.
Record what happened in the log, so the desk and housekeeping can follow up, and so that the next rooming goes well.

blocks.note: If you find a room that appears to be occupied (belongings, a person, a Do Not Disturb sign), apologise, close the door at once and call the desk. Never go in. The guest may have been given the room by mistake.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Rooming different guests and different properties

blocks.p: A group, such as a tour party or a wedding party, arrives all at once. Without a plan the lobby fills with people and bags, and the desk cannot cope.

flow: Get the rooming list and check it with the group leader before the group arrives
Check that all rooms are ready and note any special needs (ground floor, connecting rooms)
Prepare key folders in advance, labelled with names and room numbers
Welcome the group together and give one short briefing: meal times, meeting points, and where to find help
Tag the luggage by room and send it up in a planned order
Give each guest or family a folder and room number quietly
Record rooms done and report problems to the desk

ul: Hand each person their key folder quietly. Do not announce room numbers to the whole group.
Send bags up separately, tagged, so that people do not wait in the lobby. Check the count against the rooming list.
Ask older guests and guests with limited movement whether they would like a ground-floor room.
Greet by name, and thank repeat guests for returning.
Check that any amenity is placed in the room before arrival and is correct.
Follow the property's standard: do not offer extras the property does not allow.
Treat every guest with the same respect, not only VIPs.

head: Guest
How you help
rows: Guest who uses a wheelchair
Check beforehand that the route and room have no steps, and that doors, bathroom and bed suit
Walk at their pace; do not push the wheelchair unless they ask
Show where the roll-in shower, grab rails and alarm are; make sure the safe and the controls are within reach
Tell them the evacuation plan for a fire
Guest who is blind or has low vision
Say who you are; offer your arm and walk slightly ahead, telling them about steps and doors
In the room, describe the layout (bed, bathroom, wardrobe, safe) and put things in the same place
Never move things afterwards without telling them
Guest who is deaf or hard of hearing
Face the guest, speak clearly (do not shout), offer to write things down
Tell the desk so that a flashing alarm or a written wake-up can be arranged
Older guest, or someone who walks slowly
Offer a ground-floor room if one is free; go slowly; offer your arm; point out seats on the way
Guest on crutches or with a walking aid
Take the lift, not the stairs; carry the guest's other bags; keep the way clear
Family with young children
Show the cot or extra bed, baby gate or socket covers if requested; point out pool rules and balcony locks
Warn that small items and the minibar need to be out of reach
Guest with a food allergy
Make sure the kitchen and desk know; tell the guest who to ask about meals

blocks.p: At a villa the guest may be the only guest, with a whole house and grounds to learn. Rooming becomes a **welcome tour**. The staff may be few, and you may be the cook, the housekeeper and the host on the same day.

head: Villa topic
What you show or explain
rows: Gate, locks and alarm
How to open and close the gate, lock doors, and set and switch off the alarm; who to call if it goes off.
Pool and outdoor areas
Pool rules (no diving in shallow water, children supervised, no glass at the pool edge), the pool hours and safety equipment.
Staff
Introduce the cook, housekeeper, gardener and security, and say how and when to ask for them.
House features
Kitchen, laundry, air conditioning, fans, hot water, water tank and pump, generator or backup power if there is one.
Bedrooms
Which bedroom for whom; the cot or extra bed; the safes; the bathrooms.
Emergency
The emergency numbers, first aid kit, fire exits and extinguisher, the nearest clinic.
House rules
Noise, visitors, parties, smoking, and anything else the owner's rules say.
Meals and services
Mealtimes, how to order, and how to arrange a tour or a driver.

blocks.note: Water lock-offs and power cuts happen in Jamaica. At a villa, show guests where the water tank, pump switch and torches are, and tell them what to expect and who to call.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.h: Keeping the guest and the room safe and private

ul: Never say a room number aloud in public. Show it written on the folder.
Do not give guests' names or room numbers to visitors or callers.
Never leave a guest's luggage unattended in the lobby or the corridor.
Never let anyone into a guest's room except as the property's rules say.
Do not enter a room when the guest is inside unless invited, except in an emergency.
Show how to lock the door and the balcony, how to use the chain and the peephole, and where the safe is.
Tell the guest the fire plan and the nearest exit. In the room, point to the plan inside the door.
Lift correctly, use the trolley for heavy luggage, and take care with wet floors and steps.
Report spills and hazards in corridors. Do not leave trolleys or bags where people can trip.
If you are alone with a guest in a room, keep the door open, and behave professionally.
Never accept an invitation to join a guest for drinks when on duty: thank them politely and say you must stay on duty.

blocks.p: Guests may offer a tip. Thank them, and follow the property's tipping policy (some properties pool tips or have a service charge). Never ask for one.

head: Record
What it contains
Why
rows: Rooming slip or bell log
Room number, time, number of bags, and your name.
So the desk can trace who roomed whom, and when, if a bag is lost or a guest asks.
Faults and housekeeping problems
What was wrong and where.
So maintenance and housekeeping can fix it, and the room is not sold broken.
Special occasions and preferences
An anniversary, a birthday, allergies or any special need the guest mentioned.
So the desk can note it on the guest's profile and the property can follow up.
Complaints and requests
What the guest said and what you did.
So a supervisor can follow up.
Lost or found items
What, where and when.
So it can be returned.

ul: If guests tell you they are celebrating, congratulate them and tell the desk so it can be noted.
Return the luggage trolley and the unused tags, and report any damage to bags noted at the start.
Check back with the desk to confirm the room is now recorded as occupied.
I can explain what rooming is and why it matters.
I can read the arrivals list and prepare for special requests.
I can explain the room status codes (VC, VD, OC, OOO) and check that a room is clean and inspected.
I can greet a guest by name, introduce myself and take the key folder without saying the room number aloud.
I can count, tag and load luggage, and lift safely with my knees bent and my back straight.
I can walk the guest to the room, point out facilities and use the lift politely.
I can knock, open the room, place the luggage on the rack and step aside.
I can explain the key card slot, the air conditioning, the safe, the phone, Wi-Fi, the minibar, the locks and the fire plan.
I can deal with a room that is not ready, the wrong beds or a fault, with an apology and a call to the desk.
I can organise the rooming of a group and take care of guests with special needs.
I can show a villa guest the gate, alarm, pool rules, staff and emergency information.
I can leave the room correctly, and record the rooming and report faults and special occasions.

terms: Taking a guest to the room and showing and explaining it.
The list of guests due today, with times and special requests.
A guest who arrives without a booking.
A list of which room each member of a group will have.
Vacant and clean: the room is empty and cleaned.
Vacant and dirty: empty but still to be cleaned.
A room that cannot be sold because it needs repair.
Two rooms side by side with a door between them.
A folding extra bed on wheels.
The folder holding the key card, with the room number written on it.
The staff member who carries guests' luggage.
A lift for staff and luggage, not for guests.
A label showing the guest's name and room.
The small lens in the door to see who is outside.
The booklet of services, phone numbers and menus kept in the room.
A sign asking staff not to knock or enter.
A phone call from the desk to wake a guest at a set time.
The time by which guests must leave their room.
A small welcome extra, such as fruit or a card.

c1.title: Mr and Mrs Anderson's afternoon arrival
c1.text: At a hotel in Ocho Rios, the arrivals list shows Mr and Mrs Anderson and their toddler arriving at 3:00 p.m. They have asked for a baby cot, a ground-floor room and a note says it is their wedding anniversary. It is 2:15 p.m. Room 118, on the ground floor, is shown on the system as VD. Trainee bell attendant Marlon is checking the arrivals list.

c2.title: Luggage for Mr Brown
c2.text: Mr Tyrone Brown arrives at a Montego Bay hotel with four pieces: two heavy suitcases, a garment bag and a box of glass souvenirs marked fragile. He says he will carry his laptop bag himself. Bell attendant Omar is loading the trolley. While counting the bags with Mr Brown, he notices a long scratch on one suitcase.

c3.title: Ms Ricketts and Room 305
c3.text: Kerry-Ann, a bell attendant at a Kingston hotel, takes Ms Alicia Ricketts to Room 305. She has the key folder from the desk. She knocks and opens the door. The air conditioning is off, the room is warm, and the key card slot by the door is empty. Ms Ricketts says she has a laptop and some jewellery, and asks about the safe.

c4.title: A church group in Mandeville
c4.text: A church group of 14 people is arriving at a Mandeville guest house at 4:00 p.m. for a weekend retreat. The group leader, Pastor Hall, has sent a rooming list. Three of the group are over 75 years old, and one lady walks with a stick. The guest house has two floors and one small lift.

c5.title: A family arrives at a Port Antonio villa
c5.text: The Whittaker family (two adults, a boy of 5 and a girl of 8) arrive at a private villa in Port Antonio at 2:00 p.m. The villa has a gate with a code, an alarm, a swimming pool without a fence and a cook who starts work at 7:00 a.m. The booking says the boy is allergic to peanuts. Villa host Delroy meets them.

c6.title: A guest who cannot see
c6.text: Mr Winston Palmer, who is blind, arrives alone at a Negril hotel with one suitcase and a white cane. Bell attendant Shanice is asked to room him in Room 212, on the second floor. He says he has stayed in hotels before and likes to learn his room quickly.

questions.q: What does the code VD beside Room 118 tell Marlon?
o: Out of order: the room is closed until it is repaired
Vacant and dirty: the room is empty but not yet cleaned
Vacant and clean: the room is empty and ready to be sold
Occupied and dirty: a guest is in the room and it is untidy
questions.why: VD means vacant and dirty: nobody is in the room, but it has not been cleaned yet. A room is not ready to receive a guest until it is cleaned and inspected.

questions.q: It is 2:15 p.m. What should Marlon do about Room 118?
o: Tell the desk now, so it is cleaned and checked or swapped
Take the Andersons there at 3:00 and ask them to wait while housekeeping cleans it
Clean the room himself and put the cot in without telling anyone at the desk
Leave it until the family arrive, then ask the guests what they would prefer to do
questions.why: Problems with a room must be reported before the guest arrives, so housekeeping can finish and inspect it or the desk can choose another ground-floor room. Never take a guest to a room that is not ready.

questions.q: The toddler will sleep in the cot. What should Marlon check about it when the room is prepared?
o: That it has been put in the corner furthest from the door
Clean and safe, with a clean mattress and sheet
That it matches the colour of the other furniture in the room
That it has been marked with the hotel's name tag on the rail
questions.why: A cot is for a baby or toddler to sleep in, so it must be clean and safe: undamaged, steady, with a clean mattress and linen. It is put in place when the room is prepared, before the family arrives.

questions.q: Marlon sees the anniversary note on the arrivals list. What is the best action?
o: Buy flowers himself and put them in the room without telling anyone
Mention it aloud in the lobby so that other staff can congratulate them
Say nothing, since the guests have not asked for anything special
Tell the desk and housekeeping, so an extra can be arranged if allowed
questions.why: Special occasions are passed to the desk and housekeeping so the property can mark them as its standard allows. Buying extras yourself or announcing it in public is not the property's way.

questions.q: How should Omar load Mr Brown's bags on the trolley?
o: Garment bag first, then the cases on top so that it stays nice and flat
Heavy cases at the bottom, garment bag and fragile box on top
Fragile box at the bottom, so the heavy cases cannot slide off the trolley
Any order, as long as the whole load is tied on with a luggage strap
questions.why: Heavy items go at the bottom and light or fragile ones on top, so that they are not crushed and the load stays steady. The fragile box should also be handled with extra care.

questions.q: Mr Brown wants to carry his laptop bag himself. What should Omar do?
o: Insist on carrying it, because the property's rule is that staff take every bag
Take it and lock it in the luggage room until later
Let him carry it, and take the other bags
Ask him to put it on the trolley, so the bags travel together
questions.why: Respect the guest's wish. Many guests keep laptops, medicine and valuables with them. Carry the other bags and count them with him.

questions.q: What should Omar do about the scratch on the suitcase?
o: Say nothing, since it may have come from the flight
Rub it with a cloth and hope it does not show
Tell Mr Brown it was there when he arrived at the desk
Point it out to Mr Brown now, and note it on the log
questions.why: Checking the bags with the guest and noting existing damage protects both sides. If a bag is later said to be damaged by staff, the record shows what the bag looked like at the start.

questions.q: With all the bags on, the trolley is piled higher than Omar's eyes. What should he do?
o: Lean the load against his chest and hold the top case with one hand
Make two trips, so that he can see ahead and the load is steady
Push slowly and ask the guest to walk in front and shout warnings
Take the lift down the wide corridor, where he is less likely to meet anyone
questions.why: An overloaded or unsteady trolley can tip, hit people and injure you. If you cannot see over the load, split it into two trips. Safe lifting and loading protect you, the guest and the bags.

questions.q: The room is warm and the key card slot is empty. What should Kerry-Ann do?
o: Put the key card in the slot and show how it switches the power on
Call maintenance at once, since the air conditioning must be broken here
Open the windows and the balcony door, so the room cools down naturally
Tell her the room will cool down in a little while without any help
questions.why: Many rooms need the key card in the slot to switch on lights and air conditioning. Showing how it works prevents a false complaint about a fault, and it is one of the first features to explain.

questions.q: Ms Ricketts asks about the safe. What is the correct way to explain it?
o: Tell her to use the front desk safe instead, because room safes are never secure
Set the code for her, and write it on the key folder so that she cannot forget it
Show her how to set her own code, and look away
Point out where the safe is, and leave her to read the instructions on the door
questions.why: The guest chooses and enters her own code in private, and the staff member never sees it. Writing a code on a folder or watching the keypad would put her valuables at risk.

questions.q: The room safe does not open when Kerry-Ann tries it. Ms Ricketts has jewellery to store. What is best?
o: Report the fault, and offer another room or the desk's deposit box
Tell her to leave the jewellery in her suitcase until the safe has been repaired
Keep the jewellery herself until the safe is working again, to be safe
Try opening the safe with a spare key from the housekeeper's cart in the corridor
questions.why: A guest with valuables needs a working safe. Report the fault, and offer a solution that keeps the jewellery safe, such as another room or the desk's safe deposit box. Staff should never hold a guest's valuables personally.

questions.q: Ms Ricketts says she feels nervous alone in a hotel. What is the best help Kerry-Ann can give?
o: Tell her not to worry, as the hotel has never had a problem with its guests
Give her the phone number of a friend of Kerry-Ann's who lives nearby
Show the lock, chain and peephole; say to check callers with the desk
Stay in the room until she has unpacked and gone to bed for the night
questions.why: Showing how to use the lock, chain and peephole, and telling her to verify any caller with the front desk, gives practical help. Waiting in the room or sharing personal contacts is not professional.

questions.q: What should the staff do first to prepare for the church group?
o: Check the rooming list with Pastor Hall and label the key folders
Send all the bags up first and find out who owns each of them later
Ask the whole group to line up by age in the lobby before giving out keys
Wait at the desk and hand out rooms one by one as the guests arrive in
questions.why: A group needs a plan: check the list with the leader, check the rooms, and prepare labelled key folders so that rooming is quick and orderly. Without this the lobby becomes crowded and slow.

questions.q: What is the best way to help the three guests over 75 and the lady with the stick?
o: Put them with the rest in whichever rooms are on the list
Offer ground-floor rooms if free, and give them the lift first
Ask them to take the stairs slowly, to save the lift for the bags
Tell them to wait in the lobby until all other guests are roomed
questions.why: Older guests and those with limited mobility should be offered rooms they can reach easily, and be helped first in the lift. Ask them, rather than assuming, and tell the desk if a room change is needed.

questions.q: How should the room numbers be given to the group?
o: Ask the group leader to phone the numbers to each person in turn
Give each person a folder with the number written on it
Read out every name and room number from the lobby, to save time
Pin the whole rooming list on the notice board near the lift for everyone
questions.why: Giving each guest a folder with the number written on it keeps room numbers private, as it does for single guests. A public list tells everyone who is in which room.

questions.q: The villa pool has no fence and there are two young children. What should Delroy do?
o: Tell the parents adults must watch the children, and explain the pool rules
Tell the children firmly not to go near the water, and then leave them
Say nothing, because the parents can see for themselves that the pool is open
Lock the pool gate and keep the key with him for the rest of the stay
questions.why: Unfenced water is a real danger for young children. Explain the pool rules and that children must be watched by an adult, and tell the parents where the safety equipment is. Do it politely, as part of the welcome tour.

questions.q: How should the boy's peanut allergy be dealt with?
o: Write it on the booking only, and trust the cook to read the booking
Ask the parents to bring their own food for the boy for the week
Tell the cook and note it, so every dish and snack is checked
Leave it to the parents to remind the cook at each of the meals
questions.why: An allergy must reach everyone who prepares food: the cook is told before the family arrives, it is noted where staff will see it, and every dish and snack is checked. Relying on a booking note alone is not enough.

questions.q: What should Delroy show the family about the gate and the alarm?
o: Nothing at this point, since they can ask later if they want to know
How both work, and who to call if the alarm goes off
Only that an alarm exists, so that they know not to touch it
The gate code only, because the alarm is always set by the staff
questions.why: Guests need to open the gate and, where they are in charge of the house, to set and switch off the alarm. Show them, and give the phone number to call if it goes off.

questions.q: How should Shanice guide Mr Palmer to his room?
o: Take his cane and carry it with the suitcase, so that he is free to walk
Walk quickly ahead and call out directions to him as she goes along
Hold his hand and steer him along by the shoulders so he does not stray
Say who she is, offer her arm and warn him of steps and doors
questions.why: Introduce yourself, offer your arm and let him hold it, walk slightly ahead and say what is coming: steps, doors, lift. Never take a guest's cane or grab him.

questions.q: In the room, what is the best way to help Mr Palmer learn the layout?
o: Switch off the lights, which makes the room feel cooler and more restful
Describe where things are, and keep them in the same place
Say nothing, because he has stayed in other hotels and will manage
Move the furniture to the middle of the room so everything is easy to reach
questions.why: Describing the layout in order, and then keeping everything in the same place, helps a blind guest move about safely. Moving furniture or items later without telling him could cause an accident.
